t: The Most Effective Way To Manage Students With ADHD
q: It's to be great at classroom management. It's to double-down on the approach we recommend here at SCM.
Because this will always have the greatest impact on students with ADHD—their improvement, contentment, and ability to focus and really enjoy school. It’s not even close.
You see, no other strategy, including those I’m going to recommend as part of a future e-guide, will have much effect until and unless the first is accomplished.
But when placed in the right environment, many will quietly assimilate into the calm and well-behaved culture just like everyone else—and without extra attention from the teacher.
There is an epidemic of students who are misunderstood, labeled, pigeonholed, over-managed, and in some cases, even misdiagnosed due to poor classroom management.
But it isn’t worth much unless you create the conditions through which all students can overcome their behavioral and academic challenges.

t: Why Your Humor Isn't Working In Your Classroom
q: If you care too much and overthink it, you’ll lose your spontaneity. You’ll lose your timing and playfulness, your cleverness and quirkiness.
A classroom is a target-rich environment and by simply being aware and open-minded, what to say or do at the right moment will come to you without conscious thought.
But even professional comedians have to spend months, sometimes years, on their material, working out the perfect timing, pacing, and word choice just to get a reliable laugh.
When you try to be cool or speak to students on their level, using their lingo, attitudes, or sensibilities, it never works.
One of the tenets of improvisational comedy, which is the true secret to bringing more humor to your classroom, is to not try to be funny.
Just focus on enjoying your students and the laughs, the easy rapport, the likability, the love of being in your class . . . Will happen naturally.

t: A Simple Way To Build Rapport With Challenging Students
q: There is a strategy that builds strong, behavior-influencing rapport with virtually any student.
It’s about your genuine desire to get to know them, nothing more.
But you must have no ulterior motive, no hidden agenda, no strings attached. Because if you do, if you think of it as a strategy to get something from them, they’ll know it.
Be direct and refrain from using praise or flattery to try to get them to open up. This is a common tactic that communicates loud and clear that you do, in fact, have an ulterior motive.
In time, you’ll discover common interests and be drawn into wanting to learn more and more about them. Inevitably, they’ll also become curious about you.

t: I Stopped Holding My Students Accountable And Here Is What Happened d-heres-what-happened/
q: For one week, I decided to no longer rely on my classroom management plan. That's right. I just stopped following it.
By Wednesday morning, it was clear that their opinion of me had dropped a few notches.
My leverage and influence was fading before my eyes and my leadership presence was fading before theirs.

One thing I found especially interesting about the experiment, and heartening, frankly, was that as the week went on more and more students approached me to ask variations of, “What are you doing?” “Why are you doing this?” and “Are you okay?
Done right, as we recommend here at SCM, accountability is a powerful force for good. It’s a wonderful benefit for students and indispensable to creating a happy and well-behaved class.
